title: Two Sum
candidateDescription: You have a list of numbers and a target value. Write a function that finds two numbers in the list that add up to the target. You can assume there's always exactly one valid answer, and you can't use the same number twice.
interviewerContext:
Two Sum. Constraints: 2 <= nums.length <= 10^4, integers can be negative or positive, exactly one solution exists, cannot use the same element twice. Return the indices of the two numbers.

What the optimal path looks like: candidate recognizes a hash map lets them trade space for a single pass -- store each value and its index, check for the complement on the way. O(n) time, O(n) space. Brute force is O(n^2) with two nested loops.

Natural ambiguity for clarifying: the description intentionally omits what to return -- let the candidate ask or state their assumption. If they ask, tell them indices. If they say they will return the values instead, redirect them to return indices.

Probing cues (use when candidate stalls or submits brute force):
- What if you could look up whether a number exists in O(1) -- how would that change your approach?
- You are iterating through the array already -- what information could you be storing as you go?
- Your solution works -- what is the time complexity, and do you see a way to bring it down?

Strong answer: states the hash map idea unprompted or arrives there quickly when nudged, explains why it works in one pass, mentions O(n) / O(n). Weak answer: jumps straight to nested loops, does not recognize the space/time tradeoff, or cannot articulate complexity.

title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
candidateDescription: Given a string, find the length of the longest contiguous part of it where no character appears more than once.
interviewerContext:
Longest substring without repeating characters. String length up to 5 * 10^4, can contain any ASCII including spaces.

What the optimal path looks like: sliding window with a hash map tracking the last-seen index of each character. On a repeat, jump the left boundary to just past the previous occurrence (don't just increment by one — candidate must not move left backward). O(n) time, O(min(n, alphabet)) space.

Natural ambiguity for clarifying: 'contiguous' may prompt a question about whether substrings must be consecutive — yes. Spaces and special characters are valid characters. Accept these as clarifying questions.

Probing cues:
- 'Walk me through what happens to your window when you hit a repeated character.'
- 'What if the repeated character's previous occurrence is behind your left pointer — do you still move?'
- 'Your two-pointer approach is right — what are you storing inside the window to check for repeats quickly?'

Strong answer: arrives at sliding window, correctly handles the left-pointer-not-moving-backward trap (the 'abba' case), explains O(n). Weak answer: O(n^2) nested loop checking each substring, or sliding window but with incorrect left pointer update that moves it backward.

hiddenTestCases.description: left pointer must not move backwards

Define a new function `def longest_k_distinct(s, k):` for this — it will be graded instead of `length_of_longest_substring`; your existing code can stay.

title: Course Schedule
candidateDescription: A student needs to complete a set of courses. Some courses have prerequisites — you must finish one before you can take another. Given the total number of courses and a list of prerequisite pairs, determine whether it's possible for the student to finish all of them.
interviewerContext:
Course Schedule — topological feasibility / cycle detection. Up to 2000 courses, up to 5000 prerequisite pairs. Each pair [a, b] means b must come before a.

What the optimal path looks like: model as a directed graph. The question reduces to: does a valid topological ordering exist? Equivalently, is the graph acyclic? Two valid approaches — Kahn's algorithm (BFS with indegree tracking) or DFS cycle detection with a 'currently visiting' set. Both O(V+E). The graph may be disconnected; all components must be acyclic.

Natural ambiguity for clarifying: candidate may ask whether prerequisites can be circular in the input (yes, that's what you're detecting), or whether a course can have multiple prerequisites (yes). Good clarifying questions.

Probing cues:
- 'How would you model the prerequisite relationships — what does the data structure look like?'
- 'You've built the graph — what property of it tells you whether the student can finish?'
- 'Your DFS is finding a cycle — how are you distinguishing a node you finished visiting from one you're currently in the middle of?'

Strong answer: independently frames it as cycle detection on a directed graph, picks a correct algorithm and explains the visited/in-progress distinction for DFS (or indegree approach for Kahn). Weak answer: tries to simulate the schedule directly without graph framing, or uses undirected cycle detection (wrong for directed graphs).

followUps.prompt: Now instead of just true or false, return one valid order to take all the courses — or an empty list if it's not possible. If multiple valid orders exist, return the lexicographically smallest one. Define a new function `def find_order(num_courses, prerequisites):` for this — it will be graded instead of `can_finish`; your existing code can stay.

title: Coin Change
candidateDescription: You have coins of various denominations and you can use as many of each as you want. Given a target amount, find the minimum number of coins needed to make exact change. If it's not possible, return -1.
interviewerContext:
Coin Change — unbounded knapsack / bottom-up DP. Up to 12 coin types, values up to 2^31-1, amount up to 10^4.

What the optimal path looks like: bottom-up DP table where dp[a] = fewest coins to make amount a. Initialize dp[0] = 0, rest to infinity. For each amount, try every coin. O(amount * len(coins)) time, O(amount) space. Greedy is provably wrong — classic counterexample: coins [1,3,4], amount 6. Greedy picks 4+1+1=3 coins; DP finds 3+3=2.

Natural ambiguity for clarifying: candidate may ask if coins can be reused (yes, unlimited), whether amount can be 0 (yes, answer is 0), or whether there's always a solution (no, return -1 if not). All good clarifying questions.

Probing cues:
- 'Would a greedy approach work here — always picking the largest coin that fits?'
- 'You're building up to the amount — what does each cell in your table represent, and how does a smaller subproblem feed into a larger one?'
- 'What's the base case, and what do you initialize the rest of the table to?'

Strong answer: recognizes greedy fails with a concrete example, arrives at DP framing independently, correctly sets up recurrence and initialization. Weak answer: attempts greedy without questioning it, or sets up recursive solution without memoization (exponential), or initializes dp[0] incorrectly.

followUps.prompt: Instead of the count, return the actual list of coins you used to make the amount, sorted in descending order. If the amount can't be made, return an empty list. Define a new function `def coin_change_path(coins, amount):` for this — it will be graded instead of `coin_change`; your existing code can stay.

hiddenTestCases.description: greedy trap — taking the largest coin first uses more coins
zero amount — empty list of coins
single coin makes the exact amount
impossible amount — smaller than every coin

title: Number of Islands
candidateDescription: You're given a grid of 1s and 0s, where 1 is land and 0 is water. Cells connect horizontally and vertically. Count how many distinct islands there are.
interviewerContext:
Number of Islands. Grid up to 300x300. An island is a connected component of 1s using 4-directional adjacency (not diagonal).

What the optimal path looks like: DFS or BFS flood fill — iterate over every cell, when you hit an unvisited 1 increment the count and flood-fill the whole connected component (marking visited to avoid recounting). O(m*n) time and space. Union-Find is also valid and worth discussing as an alternative.

Natural ambiguity for clarifying: candidate may ask about diagonal connections (not connected), whether the grid can be empty (handle it), whether they can modify the input (acceptable, but worth mentioning). All reasonable clarifications.

Probing cues:
- 'You've found a land cell — how do you make sure you don't count parts of the same island twice?'
- 'Walk me through what happens when your DFS reaches the edge of the grid or a water cell.'
- 'What's the space complexity of your DFS approach — what's on the call stack in the worst case?'

Strong answer: frames it as connected components, picks DFS/BFS cleanly, handles visited state correctly (marking cells or using a set), discusses diagonal non-adjacency if not told. Weak answer: tries to count 1s without flood filling, confuses connected components with individual cells, or uses diagonal adjacency.

followUps.prompt: Now imagine the grid isn't given all at once — land cells arrive one at a time as coordinate updates. Your function now takes the grid dimensions and the updates, where positions is a list of [row, col] cells that turn to land in order. Return a list with the island count after each update; an update may repeat a cell that's already land, which leaves the count unchanged. Define a new function `def num_islands_stream(rows, cols, positions):` for this — it will be graded instead of `num_islands`; your existing code can stay.
